front: Give three echo features of acute pulmonary embolism.
back: 1) RV dilation (RV/LV basal ratio > 1). 2) McConnell's sign (RV free-wall akinesis with apical sparing). 3) Septal flattening in systole (D-shaped LV). Also reduced TAPSE, moderately elevated TR jet velocity (typically capped ~ 3.5 m/s in acute PE).

front: What is the '60/60 sign' and what does it suggest?
back: Pulmonary AT < 60 ms AND TR peak gradient < 60 mmHg — suggests acute pulmonary embolism. The RV is unable to acutely generate high pressures against elevated PVR.

front: Definitive treatment for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension?
back: Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE) — surgical removal of organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. Riociguat and balloon pulmonary angioplasty are options for inoperable disease.

front: What condition should be suspected when a bubble study shows delayed (> 3 cardiac cycles) appearance of bubbles in the LA?
back: An intrapulmonary shunt — most commonly a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation. Frequently associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu).

front: State a common finding on echo that helps distinguish COPD from constrictive pericarditis.
back: COPD shows marked INSPIRATORY INCREASE in SVC forward flow (from exaggerated negative pleural pressure), whereas in constrictive pericarditis the SVC flow is minimally variable with respiration. Also, transmitral inflow is not restrictive in COPD.

front: What percentage of chronic PE patients develop CTEPH?
back: ~2–4% of survivors of acute PE develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
